Understand the compiler, request runtime, generation lifecycle and package boundaries.

ZeruxJS is a Node server runtime that discovers application modules and combines them with explicit plugin registration. Its most useful organizing idea is a runtime generation : a prepared collection of routes, middleware, workers, service managers and configuration that can serve requests together.

sections: ZeruxJS connects file routes, middleware, controllers, plugins and background workers. Applications return HTML, JSON, redirects or streams. The server lifecycle initializes shared services and coordinates development reloads.

The repository is at 0.0.3 and remains early development. The create-zerux-js scaffolder currently provides help and version output only. React, Vue and Zyro integration packages exist, but package presence does not imply a complete rendering adapter. These docs distinguish implemented runtime APIs from future plans.

Begin with Installation and Routing, then add middleware and plugins. Use Workers for background services, Services for shared managers, and Deployment for production builds. The package directory records every public package and its actual export paths.

Start with [installation](installation.md), run the [notes tutorial](tutorial.md), then read the [runtime mental model](mental-model.md). Add one service at a time from the [configuration handbook](configuration-reference.md). This ordering lets you distinguish route/module errors from an unavailable database or queue before several failures interact. The framework coordinates application startup, file discovery, request dispatch, plugins and owned services. Focused packages also work outside that runtime, but a standalone factory does not inherit application configuration or shutdown automatically. The package directory shows the implementation contract for each installed release, including honest placeholder status for future CMS/generator packages.

An ESM JavaScript application can export a JSDoc-typed zerux.config.js ; a TypeScript application can use zerux.config.ts with satisfies ZeruxConfig . Both configure the same runtime. Neither a type annotation nor package installation automatically enables a database, authentication policy, React renderer or static-export pipeline. Use the [TypeScript chapter](typescript.md) for strict checks, public option inference, request contexts and browser/server boundaries. Treat request bodies and environment variables as untrusted runtime inputs even when the surrounding application is fully typed.

The current create packages are placeholders, so manual setup is the supported starting path. The docs site itself is a static exporter using workspace packages; its configuration's documentation namespace is not a built-in general-purpose static-site feature. Read [capabilities](capabilities.md) and each guide's lifecycle/failure section before interpreting a roadmap or README headline as a completed integration.

Layer Responsibility Examples --- --- --- Application Domain behavior, authentication, authorization and HTML app/ , middleware/ , plugins/ Framework Discovery, request dispatch, build, generation lifecycle zeruxjs Ecosystem Focused reusable capabilities, often independently usable @zeruxjs/cache , @zeruxjs/files , @zeruxjs/search Using a package independently does not register it with your runtime. Some services support configuration-driven startup; others are explicitly constructed and registered by application code.

1. Load project configuration and resolve source directories. 2. Initialize database/cache and optional managed services. 3. Discover middleware, controllers, composables and file routes. 4. Run plugins and the optional entry module to register extensions. 5. Seal the runtime's route set and register reserved service endpoints. 6. Start managed workers before accepting application traffic. A startup failure must release resources already initialized. Workers should return cleanup functions. Service managers have their own close/disconnect contracts.
A request's route through the system

Host checks happen before application dispatch. The protocol gateway and public-file handling occur before the normal middleware-driven route path. For application routes, the runtime parses request state, runs global middleware, applies registered multisite mappings, selects a matching route, runs route middleware and serializes the result. [Request lifecycle](request-lifecycle.md) explains the boundaries that matter for security.

Development builds a candidate generation before activation. A failed candidate does not replace the last working handler. Old workers and service resources have lifecycle cleanup; keep custom resources inside that ownership model. A process-global connection started at module import bypasses it.

The framework compiler emits application JavaScript and a build manifest. The running Node server executes those modules when handling requests. This documentation app instead renders a finite set of known content routes to HTML during its own build. That exporter is app-specific, not a generic framework static-export feature.

The project has React/Vue observable bridges and Zyro libraries, but the server runtime does not automatically provide Next-style component layouts, server actions, route caches, image optimization or a complete hydration adapter. Use the [capability map](capabilities.md) to distinguish actual contracts from future integrations.
TypeScript mirrors ownership, not runtime guarantees

ZeruxConfig describes startup input, ZeruxPluginApi describes registration, and ZeruxRequestContext describes one request. These types are deliberately different owners. Do not pass a startup config with secrets into a browser state type, or assume a request-local interface makes a module-level singleton request-local. A service type argument can describe the expected cache/database facade, but the service can still be absent or degraded. Validate unknown input before crossing into a trusted service and handle its explicit failure result. A build's transpilation is not a semantic typecheck or a real backend operation.

Ask which phase owns the failure: config evaluation, environment availability, service startup, module discovery, plugin registration, route matching, request processing or shutdown. Inspect that phase's bounded diagnostics rather than restarting every backend or loosening host policy at once. During development, a failed candidate can leave the previous generation active. That is distinct from a browser cache or a missing file watcher event. During production, verify the built artifact and process root instead of assuming that a running Node process means the intended build was loaded. See [service lifecycle](service-lifecycle.md), [configuration structure](configuration-structure.md) and [deployment](deployment.md).
Use a supported Node.js version satisfying the engines field of your installed packages. CI exercises Node 22 and 24. Install dependencies with npm and keep the lockfile committed.

The [TypeScript guide](typescript.md) includes the strict NodeNext project configuration and explains why browser libraries belong only in the entry points that use them.

Then add an actual database adapter using [database configuration](configuration-database.md). A memory store in a tutorial disappears on restart and is not a production persistence plan. Keep private files outside public directories. Pass credentials through the server environment and validate required values at startup. Do not add every optional backend before the first route runs: first verify a plain response, then the service that route needs, then the production artifact.

If startup fails, distinguish a missing config/entry file, module format mismatch, unavailable service and incompatible Node/native driver before changing several settings at once.

zerux build compiles application sources; it does not perform TypeScript typechecking. The production application still needs Node and its dependencies. This is different from this documentation site's static export.

Replace the teaching store with [database access](database-queries.md), add [authentication](package-auth.md), and cache only public or appropriately scoped results with [cache](package-cache.md). Before production, define ownership, authorization, durable persistence and operational limits.

app contains file routes. middleware contains global request middleware. controllers and composables hold reusable application logic. plugins extend the runtime. public contains directly served assets.

The structure option changes discovery directories. Plugin, middleware, controller, composable and public directories can be a string or an array. An entryPoint names an optional application registration module.
The application compiler stages output beneath .zerux/build. Keep generated artifacts out of source control. The documentation app has its own static export pipeline and writes dist instead.

Routes define public entry points. Controllers/composables contain reusable server logic; plugins register runtime resources; private storage and migration files remain outside public assets. A public folder is not an appropriate place for configuration, signed tokens, database backups or user uploads that require authentication. These paths resolve from the application root. The entryPoint is a basename used for application registration, not a URL prefix. Keep module basenames unambiguous when the loader also registers shorthand names. A filesystem move can change route inference or a registry key even if TypeScript relative imports still compile.

Use a strict tsconfig whose include paths match the chosen source layout. The compiler and runtime discovery are different mechanisms: adding a folder to tsconfig does not make it a public route, and adding a file to public does not make it private TypeScript source. Use the [structure/environment reference](configuration-structure.md) for exact accepted values and startup order. Build output should be generated, disjoint from sources and reproducible from the lockfile. Verify the built module/public layout before deployment rather than copying a development working directory with secrets and caches. The docs application's dist folder is its separate static pipeline and should not be confused with runtime outDir.

Cache, search, feed, SEO, validation, file storage and many browser helpers can be used outside a Zerux application. Read package guides for runtime requirements: filesystem adapters are Node-only; focus/dialog helpers need a DOM; SMTP, Redis and object storage need external infrastructure.

Memory caches, local search indexes, hook state and local snapshots are not distributed databases. BullMQ provides durable scheduling through Redis, but handlers are at-least-once. Analytics events are best effort. Numeric aggregates report indexed-only coverage. A shared versioned document store can coordinate control-plane writes only when the underlying store provides atomic compare-and-swap.

Each docs version has its own Markdown content. Sources are linked on every page. When a feature changes, add or update the guide, reference contract, example and limitations together. Do not describe an intended capability as shipped simply because a package name exists.
TypeScript declarations are not feature activation

The public configuration type has an open extension signature. A custom or compatibility field can therefore pass a root typecheck while no runtime code reads it. The configuration handbook distinguishes managed service setup, explicit package factories and declared-but-not-universal switches. Check a nested known option type when validating a service object. A package export also describes an available function, not all of its operational prerequisites. Browser functions need a DOM, Redis processors need real Redis, and host callbacks such as authorization/persistence must be supplied by the application. A callback name in an example is not a bundled identity provider.
Evaluate a feature end to end

Start from the installed package version and its public entry point. Follow the guide's setup, run one real operation, exercise invalid input/unavailable dependencies, then verify cleanup and production output. Report which environment was exercised. Source-level type checks, injected-driver tests, a static export and a real multi-instance deployment establish different evidence. Placeholder packages intentionally document only metadata or help/version output. Do not turn roadmap language into a deployment dependency. Use the manually configured runtime, implemented package APIs and a supported hosting model until a future release supplies the missing application behavior.

The default resolver considers .env, .env.local, then environment-specific files and their local variants, using NODE_ENV or the lifecycle's default environment. Additional structure.env paths extend the set. The current loader sets process.env only when a key is undefined. The first value encountered wins , including a value already present in the process. Do not assume later .local files override earlier keys as in other frameworks. Configure deployments through the process environment and verify precedence for your application.

The built-in parser skips comments/empty lines, splits at the first equals sign, removes matching surrounding quotes and converts escaped newline sequences. It is a small parser, not a full shell evaluator. Do not assume variable expansion, command substitution or every dotenv syntax extension.

Use process.env for private configuration and context.env inside request code. Configuration and module-evaluation timing can matter when a value must be available before a manager is constructed. Avoid importing an eager client before the required environment is initialized.

Zerux does not make arbitrary process.env values safe for the browser. Never return context.env or whole startup config objects. Create an explicit allowlist of nonsecret public settings when a page needs them. Secret values must not enter documentation examples, snapshots, public assets or request logs.

Changing an environment value does not necessarily recreate an existing client or decrypt old data. Restart/rebuild the relevant lifecycle generation and follow each service's key-rotation procedure. Tracking signing-key rings, password salts and session encryption keys have different compatibility implications.

The order in the current HTTP runtime matters: 1. Begin bounded request metrics and check allowed hosts. 2. Give enabled protocol gateway endpoints a chance to handle the request. 3. Serve matched public assets. 4. Determine whether the application route needs a streamed body; otherwise parse the bounded body. 5. Create ZeruxRequestContext with fresh request state. 6. Execute global middleware and apply multisite registrations. 7. Resolve the route/method, attach params, and execute its middleware and handler. 8. Serialize the result or route a thrown error through exception handling. Public assets and gateway endpoints are not ordinary application route handlers. A global middleware check is therefore not a universal security perimeter. Gate gateway endpoints through protocol authorization and never put confidential files in public/ .

context.state is a fresh object for one request. Controllers, plugin-created objects and module globals can be shared by many requests in a process. Store authenticated identity in request state after verification, not in a mutable singleton.

Export middleware as registered middleware keys on a route, or provide them in a plugin route registration. Global middleware comes from configured middleware directories. Call await next() once to continue. Avoid sending a response and then continuing to a second writer.

The default body reader bounds application requests. JSON content is parsed; other buffered content becomes text. A route with meta.streamBody gets the original request stream instead. Once a stream is consumed it cannot be read again. Use the Fetch adapter for package HTTP helpers rather than mixing two body readers. Multisite routing has special streamed-body constraints because the final application route may be selected after middleware. Do not assume all upload routes keep their pre-match metadata under host/path rewrites; verify the target deployment and use explicit endpoint registration.

Return serializable payloads for normal handlers. createFetchRoute owns sending its Fetch response. If trusted custom code writes directly to context.res , it must finish or abort correctly and avoid returning a second payload. Disconnect-aware streaming is preferable to manually accumulating large output.

Throw HttpError(status, message, data?) for intentional HTTP failures. Avoid putting stack traces, raw SQL, credentials or rejected request payloads in public error data. Log sanitized diagnostics internally.

The context contains Node req/res as well as a URL and an unknown body. Fetch adapters construct Web Request/Response contracts; those headers/body APIs are not interchangeable with Node IncomingMessage. Use the actual exported context or inferred adapter handler type rather than a catch-all any-shaped request. Validate route/query/body values before database/file/tool operations. An authenticated identity must still be authorized for the tenant and action. Context state is per request, but a singleton controller or manager can be shared; avoid storing per-user mutable state in shared modules.

Protocol and public handling can precede global application middleware. A private file placed under public cannot be made safe merely by adding later middleware. Protocol authorization and service dashboard callbacks have their own boundaries. Test each exposed endpoint using the actual transport and method.

After a handler commits headers, errors and disconnects require cleanup rather than an unrelated replacement JSON response. Stop downstream streams/requests and preserve cancellation as cancellation. Let a generation own shared managers until old requests drain; closing a pool after one request can break other users. Verify normal completion, deliberate errors, malformed bodies, denied identity, a cancelled stream and an unsuccessful reload. Observe whether the owning resources close and whether the old active generation remains available when replacement preparation fails.
Runtime settings, not just site metadata

The config file owns database connections, cache, managed services, workers, host policy and application structure. The runtime server loads it and initializes configured services before application modules run. Importing the file alone does not initialize those services. The documentation site's static exporter consumes only its custom documentation namespace and does not start the server runtime.
Use ZeruxConfig for editor support. allowedDomains limits application hosts; configure real deployment hosts. Development domains and ports belong to your own environment.

The loader considers .env, .env.local and environment-specific variants. Keep secret values out of configuration committed to Git, logs and public responses. Read values through process.env or the runtime environment context.

Configuration supports database/db, cache, files, email, analytics, tags, reports, queue, protocols, theme, websocket, multisite and structure. Each service has its own startup options; consult the installed TypeScript declarations before enabling it.
See [zerux.config.js](zerux-config.md) for an ESM JavaScript example, file precedence, environment timing and the documentation app configuration.

Use the [configuration handbook](configuration-reference.md) rather than guessing a top-level key from a package name. Managed services are database, cache, files, email, analytics, tags, reports and queue. Other packages are explicitly initialized in plugins, handlers, workers or browser components. A type declaration can include compatibility/custom fields without a runtime consumer. In particular, an auth or security object does not automatically install login/CSRF/header middleware. The runtime service adapters map options into the owning package factories, and those factory shapes are not always identical to the config shapes.
Check one feature at a time

Start with structure/server policy and one working route. Add an adapter, configure its environment values, enable the service and verify one real operation. Then test its outage and shutdown behavior before adding another service. This makes a missing credential distinguishable from an import/path/type error. For TypeScript, validate nested options with NonNullable<ZeruxConfig['cache'] or the matching service field in addition to the root type. The root index signature permits custom keys, so a typo accepted at root is not evidence of correct setup. JavaScript projects can use JSDoc and checkJs for editor diagnostics.

Bootstrap strips raw private service settings from public runtime configuration. Keep the original module object server-side anyway; do not expose it through a debug route or serialize an environment object. An application-specific metadata namespace should contain only values intended for its actual consumer.

File Inferred route --- --- app/page.ts / app/about/page.ts /about app/api/health/route.ts /api/health app/blog/[slug]/page.ts /blog/:slug app/files/[...path]/route.ts Catch-all parameter below /files index, page and route path segments are removed during inference. Dynamic bracket segments become named params. Static segments sort ahead of competing dynamic segments. Query strings do not define a separate route; inspect context.query.

layout, loading, template and error are reserved filenames. They do not automatically create component-layout composition, loading boundaries or React error components. A generic Markdown/MDX document is not a route just because it is under app.

Export named HTTP methods for method-specific behavior, or a default handler for generic behavior. Explicit method handlers take precedence over a default module handler. A route module can export routePath or path to replace its inferred pattern. Keep patterns stable and avoid overlaps with reserved service paths.

A module can use a controller string to resolve a discovered controller export. Controller and composable registries include relative keys and basename shortcuts. Prefer distinct basenames and explicit keys where collisions are possible. These are application service references, not an automatic RPC mechanism.

Plugins expose default/register/plugin registration functions. The optional root entry module can expose default/register/setup/boot. They receive the plugin API while preparing the generation. Use configured directories and entryPoint to make discovery explicit; do not rely on a file outside build sources being copied automatically.

Files in configured public directories become direct URL assets. They bypass ordinary application handler middleware, so store only material intentionally public. File hosting does not run content validation or provide a private download policy.

A route may use TypeScript source with a typed ZeruxRequestContext, but a supported filename/export is still required for discovery. Adding a file to tsconfig does not register a route. ESM relative imports should describe the emitted module path, and runtime/build loaders must agree on how the module is executed. Prefer explicit GET/POST exports for method-specific APIs and the documented default handler for a general page. A reserved filename is a discovery rule, not proof that JSX/MDX, suspense or component layout composition exists. Test the output of the actual application compiler after moving or renaming a module.

Keep configuration, private storage and backups outside public roots. Controller/composable modules are reusable server code, not automatically HTTP endpoints. Avoid duplicate basenames where discovery supports shorthand registry keys; use clear folder/key ownership. When refactoring, check route inference, explicit routePath/path overrides, dynamic parameter names, imported modules and source-to-build paths. Then test a valid request, wrong method and missing path against the production handler. TypeScript can catch a broken relative import but cannot prove the intended public URL still resolves.

registerFetchRoutes registers an ALL route and marks its body as streamed. Your Fetch handler must enforce its supported methods. Ecosystem endpoint factories generally do this; a handwritten handler should return 405 with an Allow header for unwanted methods.

The handler receives (request, context) . Use the second argument for route params, authenticated request state and services. The adapter uses a neutral local origin for the Web Request URL; do not derive a public canonical domain or trusted tenant from that synthetic origin.

createFetchRoute(handler) returns a normal Zerux route handler. When using it in a file module that accepts uploads, export meta = { streamBody: true } so a buffered parser does not consume the stream first.

The bridge converts Node request bodies to Web streams and pipes response bodies back with backpressure. Disconnect cancellation propagates to the pipeline. Hop-by-hop response headers are removed. HEAD, 204 and 304 do not send response bodies.

Use this adapter for validator handlers, search HTTP handlers, feed endpoints, crawler routes and file responses. It preserves their status/header contracts; it does not provide authentication, tenant binding, rate limiting or write permission. Configure those policies before exposing a route.

app/page.ts maps to /. app/api/health/route.ts maps to /api/health. Directory parameters such as app/blog/[slug]/page.ts become named route parameters. A [...path] segment captures the remaining path. Reserved layout/loading/template/error names do not provide a React-style layout engine.
Export GET, POST and other method handlers, or a default handler. The request context exposes params, query, body, state, config, logger and services.
A module may export routePath or path to override its inferred path. Plugins can register routes through api.addRoute. Static path segments sort ahead of competing dynamic paths.

Normal requests use the buffered body parser with a bounded size. Upload routes that need streaming must explicitly export meta = { streamBody: true } and consume context.requestStream with their own limits.

Choose methods, input limits, authentication, status codes and response caching before writing a handler. A route parameter is a string from an untrusted URL, not a validated database key. Query parameters can repeat; use URLSearchParams deliberately rather than assuming one scalar value per name. This validates format, not ownership. Resolve the authenticated principal and authorize the item before reading private data. Do not place a complete service config or environment object in the returned JSON.

Ordinary handlers use the runtime's bounded buffered parser. If a route exports streamBody metadata, consume the original request stream exactly once under an explicit byte/time/cancellation policy. Do not attempt a buffered parse and then expect the original bytes to remain unread. Fetch adapters operate on Web Request; the route context also exposes Node request/response objects with different APIs.

Static paths win against competing dynamic paths, but avoid overlapping registrations that depend on subtle ordering. Explicit path overrides and plugin routes need the same method and authorization review as file routes. Test a wrong method, malformed parameter, repeated query, oversized body, deliberate HttpError and an unknown path. TypeScript context types document fields but do not narrow body from unknown automatically. Use schema parsing or explicit guards, and test the compiled route after build. Reserved layout/loading/template names are not proof of a component renderer or automatic frontend loading state.

Use public for CSS, browser JavaScript, icons and other intentionally public bytes. The runtime discovers these files and serves matching paths before normal application route dispatch. If public/logo.svg is present, it can be served as /logo.svg.

Do not put user uploads, environment files, backups, session exports or runtime snapshots in public. An authentication middleware in an application route does not turn direct public files into private downloads. Use files/media Fetch handlers with authorization for protected content.

zerux build copies supported application sources and public assets into the staged server build. It refuses symlinked sources and secret-looking file names under build sources and enforces file/count/byte limits. These checks are guardrails, not a substitute for reviewing source directories.

HTML pages must explicitly include stylesheets/scripts they need. The runtime does not automatically bundle an application component tree or optimize image/font assets. The font, SEO and asset catalog packages help with focused tasks; the application still hosts binaries and supplies correct HTML/CSP.

Its exporter copies public assets and renders known Markdown documents into dist. Directory index.html files serve nested routes directly; configure a real 404 page and avoid SPA history fallback. This app is mounted at /zeruxjs/; its generated links, assets and search URLs include that prefix. The combined ecosystem homepage owns the domain root.

TypeScript validates the path shape, not the contents of that directory. Audit the actual exported files and keep environment files, backups, source credentials and authenticated uploads outside it. A filename or signed-looking URL is not an access-control check.

The server runtime can discover configured public files; the docs exporter copies only its approved public build tree and generated assets. Neither operation automatically bundles every referenced JavaScript dependency, converts arbitrary Markdown, optimizes image bytes or provisions object storage. Generate browser CSS/JS and link the output with stable base-path-aware URLs. Use content versioning for reusable immutable assets and verify MIME/content type through the actual host. A local preview can set text/markdown while a static provider chooses another display/download behavior. Keep .nojekyll and prebuilt artifact deployment for the docs raw Markdown exports; a second site generator can otherwise change the artifact contract. Test nested paths, directory redirects, absent assets, HEAD and the configured static 404 response. A single successful homepage request does not prove fonts, modules, images or mounted documentation paths exist in the production tree.
Middleware discovered in configured middleware folders runs globally. Call and await next() to continue the chain. Keep per-request data in context.state rather than a module-level mutable object.

The loader registers modules by their relative key and basename. A route can reference a controller export, and request handlers can use context.services.controllers and context.services.composables. Prefer distinct basenames to avoid ambiguous registrations.
Authorize sensitive operations before the handler accesses private data. Returning a UI page or hiding a navigation link does not protect a route. Do not trust user-controlled headers as an identity.

A finally block runs for downstream success and failure. Store per-request values on context.state; a module variable can mix simultaneous users. Call next once, await it, and avoid writing a second response after a downstream handler has already completed the response.

Resolve and validate the session before accessing a private service or controller. Then authorize the specific tenant/resource/action; an authenticated user is not automatically an administrator. A public browser header or hidden UI link is not a principal. See [authentication/security setup](configuration-auth-security.md) for what is and is not initialized automatically. Apply body/CSRF/origin policy before unsafe side effects. When integrating a Fetch handler, keep Web Request headers separate from Node IncomingMessage headers. Return a deliberate error through the standard runtime path rather than swallowing failures and continuing with an undefined identity.

Controller/composable registration shares code, not permission. A reused controller must receive the already validated context or explicit trusted inputs. Avoid ambiguous basenames in discovery registries and avoid construction of per-request resource pools inside a controller. Test middleware ordering, early rejection, thrown downstream errors and concurrent requests. If middleware starts timers/listeners, identify who owns teardown. A request completion hook does not replace generation-level service shutdown. The [request lifecycle](request-lifecycle.md), [plugins](plugins.md) and [service lifecycle](service-lifecycle.md) explain the distinct owners.

Objects serialize to JSON. HTML-looking strings receive an HTML content type. Buffers can be returned for binary payloads. Headers and status can be managed through the underlying response when a custom integration requires it.
Import redirect and RedirectType from zeruxjs/navigation. Temporary is 307, Permanent 308, Found 302 and SeeOther 303.

HttpError and exceptionHandler are public exports. Throw errors through the runtime error path instead of exposing stack traces or secret connection details in custom JSON. Log sufficient diagnostic context while redacting credentials.
Choose a serialization and status contract

An ordinary object return is useful for JSON, but an object type does not choose all HTTP status/header semantics. Use a Fetch bridge and Response when you need a complete Web response contract, or the documented runtime response helpers for redirects, bounded streaming and caching. Avoid mixing a manually ended Node response with another returned response value. 303 changes the follow-up to a retrieval request, while 307/308 preserve method semantics. A redirect target derived from input needs an approved same-origin/allowlist policy; a typed string is not an open-redirect defense.

HTML-looking strings are not automatically sanitized. Escape user text and script-embedded JSON with the appropriate helper; HTML escaping and URL validation are different operations. An error response must not include connection passwords, raw tokens or stack traces. Preserve deliberate public status/error messages while logging a redacted diagnostic context server-side. Cache headers belong to the response's privacy model. Personalized responses should not become public merely because they are successful. A cached payload can outlive session changes; validate authorization before returning it and include tenant/data-version boundaries in cache keys. See [cache/stream responses](cache-streams.md) for header and cancellation details.

Use the exported response/stream policy types or infer an option type from the helper signature. Type checking cannot know whether headers have already been sent or a network consumer disconnected. Test GET and HEAD, deliberate HttpError, unsupported method, cancellation, redirects and conditional responses through the real runtime. A stream failure after headers are committed cannot always be converted into a fresh JSON error response. Make error and cleanup behavior explicit at the stream owner. Keep error serialization consistent so callers can distinguish invalid input, denied access, missing resources and infrastructure failure without parsing private log text.

zerux.config.js is the application's runtime configuration entry point. Its role includes database connections, cache providers, storage, email, queues, authentication/security, workers, protocols, host restrictions and file discovery. Site metadata is only an optional application extension; it is not the primary purpose of this file. The runtime server command performs these steps: 1. Load the standard environment files for the selected mode. 2. Find and evaluate the application configuration module. 3. Resolve project structure and load additional structure.env files. 4. Bootstrap the database and cache, then the other configured services. 5. Create the application runtime, including application modules and plugins. Simply importing the config object in a script does not perform these steps. The Node server startup command owns service initialization; the static site exporter does not.

Place one configuration file at the application root, alongside its package.json. The framework checks zerux.config.ts , zerux.config.js , zerux.config.mjs , then zerux.config.cjs , and uses the first existing file. It does not merge several files. If none exists, the loader returns an empty object and runtime defaults apply. Removing a configuration file therefore does not disable application discovery. For an ESM application with "type": "module" , use a default export: In a CommonJS application use zerux.config.cjs with module.exports = { ... } , or use .mjs for an unambiguous ESM file. The loader accepts default exports and the legacy named zeruxConfig / zdevConfig exports; prefer a default export for new applications. Configuration modules execute on the server, so keep imports deliberate and side effects minimal.

type selects the fix , dynamic or function structure mode. Paths such as structure.app , structure.public and outDir resolve relative to the application root. The default route folder is app , entry module basename is index , and runtime output directory is .zerux . Middleware, controller, composable and plugin settings accept discovery directories; check the [configuration reference](configuration-reference.md) for exact shapes. The nested server object owns ports and allowed-host settings. An allowed hostname does not authenticate a visitor. Database, cache, files, email and queue configuration belongs to runtime service startup; check their guides before configuring external services. Configuration changes generally require restarting the owning runtime or rebuilding its output.

The runtime uses db (or the legacy database alias) to configure the database manager. It selects the manager package through connectorManager , defaulting to @zeruxjs/db . Connection connector values select adapters such as @zeruxjs/db-pg . Install the adapter and supply the database environment values before starting this example. The memory cache is process-local and does not share data between application instances. For a standalone cache manager the option is helper ; for this runtime configuration it is connector . Database initialization runs before cache initialization. A configured database initialization failure rejects startup. Cache startup uses a three-second default timeout; required: true makes a startup failure fatal, while an optional connector initialization/timeout failure returns no cache manager after reporting the failure. Manager-package import failures and missing factory exports still propagate; required: false does not suppress every configuration error. Omitting a database or cache configuration leaves that service unconfigured. See [database queries](database-queries.md), [cache](package-cache.md) and [managed services](services.md) for ownership, cleanup

The compiler package wraps transpilation and an optional fast bundler. Transpilation removes type syntax; it is not a full typecheck. Run a separate compiler check in development and before release. For JavaScript use / @type {import('zeruxjs').ZeruxConfig} / before the default object, and enable allowJs / checkJs in a separate checker configuration if needed. The root config permits custom keys, so checking a nested known service type is more effective at finding misspelled service options than relying on the open root type alone.

This approach stays aligned with installed declarations without importing internal source files or inventing an exported Options name. Overloaded and generic factories may require more specific public types; package guides list the relevant contracts. Keep unknown at untrusted JSON boundaries and validate it before narrowing. An as cast only changes the compiler's belief.

Use the framework's exported ZeruxRequestContext and ZeruxPluginApi for application integration. Service lookup should use the concrete service type from its owning factory. TypeScript does not prove that an optional service was enabled; check the lookup result and the relevant ready/degraded state before use. Do not use a non-null assertion merely to avoid handling a missing backend. Virtual specifiers such as db:reporting are loader-owned. A plain TypeScript/Node execution does not automatically resolve them; use a real manager import in standalone scripts. Keep any custom declaration mappings local to the application's generated virtual module contract rather than hiding unresolved imports with a catch-all declare module ' ' .

Environment values are strings or undefined. Parse numeric ports/timeouts, reject missing required credentials at startup, and validate uploaded JSON, query parameters and persisted snapshots. Schema types can infer validated output, but a TypeScript interface alone cannot reject an HTTP payload. See [validation](package-validator.md) for bounded Fetch adapters.

If browser globals are missing, select the appropriate DOM libraries only for files that actually use browser APIs. If an ESM import fails, check package.json type, extension and export conditions before adding a custom loader. A passing typecheck does not connect databases, send email, test Redis or certify a browser hydration flow.

The database manager is initialized before cache and other managed services. db takes precedence over the legacy database alias. connectorManager changes the manager module and defaults to @zeruxjs/db ; each connection's connector selects a driver. The root ZeruxConfig declares auth and security , but the current core service bootstrap does not automatically turn them into a login service, CSRF protection or authorization middleware. This matters because the root type also allows custom keys: a value accepted by TypeScript is not proof that a runtime consumer reads it. Install the packages, provision session/password key material through the process environment, define the application's database schema, and add route/middleware authorization. Configuration is input; enforcement occurs where the request is authenticated and an operation is authorized.

Call this in the owning server initialization path, not a browser entry point or on every request. The package's session expiration is in seconds. Provide SECURITY_SESSION_KEY , SECURITY_SESSION_SALT and SECURITY_PASSWORD_SALT securely. There are three different lifetimes: lifecycle workers belong to one runtime generation, thread workers run registered CPU tasks, and queue workers consume durable Redis jobs. worker.minThreads and worker.maxThreads configure thread defaults; they do not make arbitrary asynchronous functions durable or create BullMQ queues. The implementation normalizes positive integer thread counts. Minimum defaults to one, and maximum defaults to at least the minimum. These are defaults used by worker registration; inspect a specific pool's options before assuming a config-level number overrides every pool. Tune against memory per worker and the cost of loading the application, not only CPU core count.

Use the framework's worker definitions and plugin registration APIs. Keep an application task's input serializable, validate it before sending to a thread, and decide what happens when the caller aborts. A thread result is not a database transaction. Avoid passing open database clients, raw request objects or secrets into a worker merely because TypeScript permits an unknown-shaped payload. Lifecycle workers should return cleanup for timers, subscriptions and owned handles. Runtime generations can overlap while old requests drain: a global singleton timer can therefore run twice unless its ownership is explicit. Queue processors need idempotency and durable state because delivery may be repeated after a crash or timeout.

Use the exported worker/context types and defineWorker / defineThreadWorker APIs rather than writing a catch-all function signature. A contextual type describes the host interface but does not guarantee the configured service is available. Check optional services and distinguish an application cancellation from a task failure.

Test success, validation failure, timeout/cancellation, worker failure and application shutdown. Measure throughput and memory at the expected concurrency. When scaling replicas, multiply the per-process thread/queue counts to obtain deployment-wide concurrency. A cache prefix or thread count does not coordinate a cluster. See the dedicated guides for real task examples and shutdown contracts.
